approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, spring — lake frozen or partly frozen
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Creek Road is plowed only as far as Bridge Creek Campground at about 9.2 miles from Leavenworth, which leaves roughly 3.5 miles of road to walk, snowshoe or ski to the Stuart Lake / Mountaineer Creek trailhead at 3,400 ft. Plan for that; it is a substantial part of the day and it is why so many parties do this route on skis.

The trail follows the creek about two miles, crosses to the west side, and continues another mile to the fork. Take the left fork, cross back, and continue southeast — about five miles from the trailhead in total — to the north end of Colchuck Lake. Campsites are on the western banks.

When the lake is frozen, cross it directly. That is the fast option and it puts you under the north face in minutes rather than an hour of shore boulders. It is also a judgement call about ice, and it stops being available once break-up starts.

Once FR 7601 opens for the season the road walk disappears and the approach shortens dramatically — but by then the couloirs are usually past their best.
approach_variants.season: Feb-Apr; the lake ice typically breaks up around mid-May
hazards: 3.5 miles of unplowed road each way in winter
Avalanche hazard on the approach and in the couloirs — this route needs a stable snowpack, not just cold
Crossing a frozen Colchuck Lake is an ice judgement, not a shortcut to take on faith
Steep, exposed snow with possible ice right at the couloir entrance, before any belay
5-9 hours one way from the lake means a benighting is a real outcome
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Triple Couloirs starts on the north face, which is not where Serpentine and Backbone start. Do not follow the moraine southwest toward the Colchuck-Dragontail col — that is the northwest face and a different set of routes.

From the lake, go counter-clockwise to the south end, then head uphill aiming just a little east (climber's east) of the lowest point of Dragontail's north face. The face has a clear low point where it meets the basin; the entrance to the first couloir — the Hidden Couloir — sits slightly east of it, around 6,400 ft.

The visible marker is a prominent snow finger running down out of the face at that point. In poor visibility, work the base of the wall until the rock stops going down and starts going up — that low point is your reference — then move a short distance east and look for the snow tongue leading up into a cleft. The entrance itself is steep, exposed snow and sometimes ice; it is narrow enough that you will know when you are in it.

The couloir is called Hidden because it does not read as a continuous line from the lake. Do not expect to see the full route from below and pick it out; find the low point of the face first, then the snow finger, then commit.

Once in, you get roughly 800 vertical feet of 40-50 degree snow and ice before the route makes any decisions — if you have climbed several hundred feet of moderate snow inside a defined cleft, you are on it.
